rv.q: This virtuoso banquet of slapstick farce and verbal jousting brings with it a shocking revelation: How starved we were for comedy.
How starved we were for comedy.
If you’re not having a good time at this show, you may be on the wrong medication.
Letting loose and neutralizing all sorts of demons, it’s ideal escapism for anxious times.
I dare you to see it and not laugh out loud, a lot.
Artisanal rib-tickling, prepared fresh, before your eyes, and a bit different every night.

There's the squeaky dry, silly-smart kind we know from Monty Python, Michael Frayn and Tom Stoppard. I love that kind. Then there is the slapstick, pants-dropping, music-hall, silly-dumb sort that traces its stock-character, low-comedy pedigree back ...
You'll know smart hilarity when you're guffawing at it.
Whatever it is, I dare you to see it and not laugh out loud, a lot.
The Music Box management should be required to install restraints for the seats, as you're likely to be falling out of yours from laughing so hard.
James Corden is a marvel of physical comedy and vocal dexterity, turning what could be a one-note farce into something approaching theatrical magic.
Hail to the clown prince of this royal scream.
It's undoubtedly the funniest, most insane show you'll find this season.
Guvnors often has you hoarse from laughing, and allows you the rare chance to brag about seeing something extremely tony that also happens to be incredibly Benny.
One Man, Two Guvnors is smart, it’s charming, and most importantly, it’s very funny!
“One Man, Two Guvnors” proves to be an extremely funny entertainment likely to banish (temporarily) whatever problems irk you.

cn.t: Critics hail this National Theatre import as a hilarious, joyously entertaining farce, with James Corden delivering a virtuosic comic performance and Nicholas Hytner's staging striking a brilliant balance between meticulous planning and anarchic spontaneity.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
